lesson.subject: data-ai
lesson.title: How AI Learns
lesson.summary: Training data and labels, patterns and testing, when AI gets it wrong, and checking its answers.
learning_objectives: Explain how a machine learns from labelled examples
Say how we test a machine and why AI can be biased
Check AI answers and use AI honestly

standards.text: Learning: computers can learn from data; machine learning uses training data and finds patterns
Societal impact: AI can impact the world in positive and negative ways, including bias

success_criteria: I can explain training data and labels
I can say why AI makes mistakes
I know how to check an AI answer
lesson.real_life: Photo apps that sort faces, voice helpers and homework helpers all learn from data and can make mistakes.

blocks.markdown: Today's big question: how does a computer learn?
blocks.say: Today we ask how a computer learns. Why does it sometimes get things wrong?

blocks.alt: Red, yellow and green-striped apples in rustic wooden crates
blocks.caption: Apples come in many colours. A machine needs to see them all.
blocks.credit: Photo by Jason Leung on Unsplash
blocks.say: These apples differ in colour, size and shape. A machine needs lots of examples to learn them all.

blocks.markdown:
**Machine learning** finds patterns in **training data**.

Nobody writes every rule. The machine learns from examples.
blocks.say: A normal program follows rules a programmer wrote. But a machine learning program works differently. Nobody writes every rule. Instead we give it lots of examples, called training data, and it finds the patterns itself. Think of teaching a child to spot a mango. You do not list rules. You show many mangoes, and say: this is a mango.

scenes.caption: Training data: pictures of fruit.
scenes.say: We show the machine pictures of fruit.

scenes.caption: Each picture has a label.
scenes.say: Each picture has a label that says what it is: mango, banana, apple. The labels are the right answers.

scenes.caption: It learns the patterns.
scenes.say: After thousands of labelled examples, the machine learns the patterns: the colour, the shape and the size. Now it can name a fruit it has never seen before.

question.explanation: Training data is the set of examples a machine learns from.

options.text: Examples we show a machine so it can learn
The rules a programmer typed in

blocks.markdown: A **label** is the right answer for an example. Wrong labels teach wrong things.
blocks.say: A label is the right answer attached to an example. If the labels are wrong, the machine learns the wrong thing. Imagine a photo of a lemon labelled as an orange. The machine would be confused. Good labels are accurate and consistent. That is why people check labels carefully.

blocks.title: A tiny labelled data set
blocks.caption: Each row is an example. The label is the fruit.

question.prompt: If a photo of a lemon is labelled as an orange, the machine could learn the wrong thing.
question.explanation: A wrong label teaches a wrong pattern.

blocks.title: Fatima trains a fruit model
blocks.transcript: Fatima shows a machine lots of fruit photos. These are the training data. Each photo has a label: the right answer. Apple. Banana. Mango. The machine finds patterns in the pictures. Nobody wrote the rules. Now she tests it with new photos it has never seen. It gets eighteen of twenty right. That is ninety percent. But it calls a green apple a lime. It only saw red apples. Narrow training data causes bias. The fix is more varied photos. Fatima checks important answers in a trusted book, and says when AI helped.
blocks.caption: Fatima trains a fruit-spotting model and finds out why it gets one wrong.

points: Machine learning learns from training data
blocks.say: Let us remember. Machine learning finds patterns in labelled training data. Good labels matter.

blocks.markdown: The machine looks for **patterns** that tell groups apart. It does not truly understand.
blocks.say: When a machine looks at lots of examples, it searches for patterns that tell the groups apart. For cats and dogs, it might spot pointed ears and whiskers on cats. Dogs have longer noses. It does not truly understand animals. It matches patterns in the numbers that make up the pictures. The more varied the examples, the better the patterns.

scenes.say: Here are some cats and dogs. The machine compares them.

scenes.caption: Patterns: ears, whiskers, noses.
scenes.say: It notices patterns: pointed ears and whiskers on one side, longer noses on the other.

scenes.caption: Now it guesses about a new picture.
scenes.say: Then it uses those patterns to guess about a new picture.

question.prompt: What does a machine learning program search for in examples?

blocks.markdown: We **test** with new examples. **Accuracy** is how many it gets right.
blocks.say: How do we know if the machine really learned? We test it with new examples it has never seen. If we tested with the same pictures it trained on, it could just remember them. Out of twenty new pictures, if it gets eighteen right, that is ninety percent accuracy. If it gets only ten right, it needs more or better training.

blocks.markdown:
**Bias** happens when training data is not varied or fair.

Machines can get things wrong if they have not seen enough different examples.
blocks.say: AI makes mistakes. Often the reason is the training data. If a machine only saw pictures of white cats, it might not recognise a black cat. That is because the examples were not varied enough. This problem is called bias. A fair machine needs training data from many kinds of examples. Also, if the world changes, old training data can go out of date.

scenes.caption: Only white cats in training.
scenes.say: The machine is trained only on white cats.

scenes.caption: A black cat. It says: not a cat?
scenes.say: Then it sees a black cat. It has never seen one like this, so it may say: not a cat.

scenes.caption: The fix: more varied examples.
scenes.say: The fix is more varied training data: cats of every colour and size.

mini_quiz.prompt: How can we make AI fairer?

blocks.text: Stop 1: Do not just trust it

blocks.markdown:
Always **check** AI answers with a trusted **source**.

Never share private details with an AI tool.
blocks.say: AI tools can sound very sure, even when they are wrong. A smart user checks. First, ask: does this make sense? Second, look for the same fact in a trusted source. A school book, an encyclopaedia or a grown-up will do. If two good sources agree, it is more likely to be right. If they disagree, keep investigating. Never share private details like your full name, address or school with an AI.

blocks.alt: Check the answer with a trusted book or a grown-up.
blocks.caption: Check the answer with a trusted book or a grown-up.

question.prompt: An AI gives you a surprising fact. What should you do?

options.text: Check it in a trusted book or with a grown-up

blocks.text: Stop 2: Using AI fairly and kindly

blocks.markdown: Be **honest** about using AI. Use it to help you think, not to think for you.
blocks.say: Using AI is also about being honest. If AI helped with your homework, say so. Copying AI answers and calling them your own is not honest. AI is a helper for learning, not a replacement for thinking. Ask it to explain, then try yourself. And remember that people matter more than machines: be kind and fair, and ask a grown-up when unsure.

blocks.alt: Be honest about when AI helps you.
blocks.caption: Be honest about when AI helps you.
blocks.say: Being fair and honest with AI means saying when it helped you.
